articles.title: Trump keeps telling Americans to ‘buy a Dell.’ His latest filing reveals his account sold up to $1M of Dell stock
articles.summary: A new ethics disclosure lists two August sales of Dell shares from the president’s account. It went public a day after he hosted Michael and Susan Dell in th...
articles.body:
President Trump says Americans should "buy a Dell," but his brokerage account sold between $500,001 and $1 million of Dell Technologies (NYSE: DELL) stock on Aug. 21, according to a federal ethics disclosure made public on Oct. 8. The same report lists a second, smaller Dell sale a week later, on Aug. 28, valued in the range of $15,001 to $50,000.

The filing came out a day after Trump hosted Dell founder Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, in the Oval Office to mark the automatic enrollment of nearly 70 million children in Trump Accounts, the children's investment program the couple has backed with a $6.25 billion pledge .

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

Trump has been one of Dell's loudest unofficial salespeople. "Go out and buy a Dell computer," he told a crowd in Rome, Georgia, on Feb. 19 — nine days after his account bought $1 million to $5 million of Dell shares , when the stock traded around $126.

The White House says the president doesn't choose the investments. Spokesman Davis Ingle told CNBC they are independently managed through discretionary accounts and computer-based models, with "no ability" for Trump or his family to influence decisions.

The Trump Organization manages the president's brokerage accounts and says third-party financial institutions oversee the trades. "Neither President Trump, his family, nor The Trump Organization plays any role in selecting, directing, or approving specific investments," the company wrote in a statement provided to Yahoo Finance.

In the months between the purchase and the sales, Dell's stock went on an absolute tear. Shares traded around $563 in late September, up about 350% for the year . But the filings list dollar ranges instead of exact figures, so they don't show what the account received for its Dell shares or how many it still owns.

What Trump's financial disclosures reveal about his Dell stock trades

Senior executive branch officials have to report stock and bond trades over $1,000 to the Office of Government Ethics within 30 days of learning about them, and no later than 45 days after the trade itself. Congress created the requirement in the STOCK Act, which President Obama signed in 2012 .

articles.title: Crédito para indústrias: 37% das empresas não obtêm financiamento | G1
articles.standfirst: Percentual de empresas que tentaram obter financiamento e não conseguiram subiu em relação a 2025; juros altos são o principal obstáculo, segundo a Confederação Nacional da Indústria.
articles.summary: Crédito para indústrias enfrenta barreiras com juros altos e exigência de garantias, segundo pesquisa da CNI sobre financiamento de longo prazo.
articles.body:
A proporção de indústrias que tentaram contratar ou renovar crédito de longo prazo, mas não conseguiram os recursos, subiu de 33% em 2025 para 37,2% em 2026. O percentual considera apenas as empresas que buscaram financiamento.

Os dados são de uma pesquisa da Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI), divulgada nesta sexta-feira (9), e se referem ao período de fevereiro a julho.

Os juros altos são o principal obstáculo para conseguir crédito. Entre as indústrias que tiveram dificuldade para obter financiamento de curto ou médio prazo, 76% citaram as taxas como uma das barreiras. No crédito de longo prazo, o percentual foi de 68,9%.

As exigências de garantias reais, como imóveis, também dificultam o acesso ao financiamento. Elas foram citadas por 33,4% das empresas com dificuldades no crédito de curto ou médio prazo e por 31,5% das que enfrentaram problemas nas operações de longo prazo.

Crédito de longo prazo para despesas do dia a dia

Parte das indústrias usa financiamentos de longo prazo para pagar despesas cotidianas, como salários e compra de insumos.

O capital de giro foi apontado como principal finalidade por 28,7% das empresas que buscaram, contrataram ou renovaram esse tipo de crédito.

O percentual ficou acima do registrado para investimentos em máquinas e equipamentos (23,6%) e construção e instalações (11,6%).

“O capital de giro, em geral, é utilizado para bancar folha de pagamento, compra de materiais, insumos, entre outras despesas do dia a dia das empresas, e já é esperado que elas busquem crédito de curto prazo para essa finalidade. Porém, chama a atenção quando elas procuram crédito de longo prazo para esse fim, porque o crédito de maior maturação costuma servir para financiar investimentos em máquinas, equipamentos e edificações, por exemplo”, afirma Maria Virgínia Colusso, analista de Políticas e Indústria da CNI.

Indústria automotiva no Sul Fluminense — Foto: Reprodução/RJ2

Entre fevereiro e julho, 49,9% das indústrias não tentaram contratar ou renovar crédito de curto, ou médio prazo. No financiamento de longo prazo, o percentual foi de 54%.

Considerando todas as empresas ouvidas, 7,5% tentaram obter crédito de curto ou médio prazo, mas não conseguiram. No longo prazo, foram 9,2%.

Entre as empresas que buscaram financiamento de longo prazo, 48,2% das pequenas e 48,1% das médias não conseguiram os recursos. Nas grandes empresas, o percentual foi de 29,9%.

A pesquisa ouviu 1.701 empresas industriais, de pequeno, médio e grande porte, entre 3 e 12 de agosto.

articles.title: Os problemas que o agro quer ver resolvidos pelo próximo presidente  | G1
articles.standfirst: Endividamento, seguro rural, eventos climáticos, infraestrutura, insumos e acesso a mercados estão entre os desafios apontados pelo setor. Especialistas afirmam que parte dos problemas exige políticas de longo prazo.
articles.summary: Endividamento, seguro rural, eventos climáticos, infraestrutura, insumos e acesso a mercados estão entre os desafios apontados pelo setor.
articles.body:
O próximo presidente vai encontrar um agronegócio que, apesar de sua importância para a economia brasileira, ainda enfrenta gargalos que não devem ser resolvidos em um único mandato.

Endividamento e crédito caro, baixa cobertura do seguro rural, perdas provocadas por eventos climáticos extremos, dificuldades de infraestrutura, dependência de insumos importados e barreiras para ampliar mercados estão entre os problemas apontados por especialistas ouvidos pelo g1 e pela Associação Brasileira do Agronegócio (Abag).

A entidade propõe cinco frentes de políticas públicas para enfrentar essas questões. Especialistas, porém, ressaltam que os desafios têm dimensões diferentes e que algumas soluções dependem de ações contínuas do governo e da iniciativa privada.

Política nacional de financiamento, seguro rural e resiliência climática da agroindústria: criação de um marco plurianual para ampliar os recursos destinados ao setor, incluindo um Fundo Nacional de Catástrofes Climáticas.

Política industrial para fortalecer as cadeias estratégicas da agroindústria brasileira: estímulo à produção de insumos, para garantir a competitividade da indústria brasileira, eliminando o "passivo regulatório" para agilizar a aprovação de novas tecnologias.

Política nacional de governança, planejamento e financiamento de infraestrutura agroindustrial: modernização e harmonização dos processos de licenciamento e autorização de empreendimentos de infraestrutura.

Política nacional de comunicação, educação e valorização da agroindústria: ações permanentes para ampliar o conhecimento sobre a contribuição do setor para a segurança alimentar, a sustentabilidade, a inovação e o desenvolvimento econômico.

Política nacional de inserção internacional e defesa da competitividade brasileira: enfrentamento de barreiras tarifárias e não tarifárias, com atuação coordenada entre governo, instituições de pesquisa e setor produtivo.

Entenda o cenário de cada um dos cinco pontos e quais caminhos para enfrentá-los.

Para Felippe Serigati, pesquisador da Fundação Getulio Vargas ( FGV ) Agro, o principal gargalo do financiamento e do seguro rural é o custo. Segundo ele, os juros permanecem elevados devido ao endividamento dos produtores e ao aumento dos pedidos de recuperação judicial.

Por este motivo, os bancos estão mais seletivos na concessão de crédito.

Leandro Gilio, pesquisador do Insper Agro Global, explica que a inadimplência dos produtores acontece por causa dos prejuízos acumulados em safras seguidas, provocados por problemas climáticos, juros altos e custos elevados de produção.

"Isso vai tendo um efeito em cadeia, prejudicando os investimentos antes da produção. Por isso que, nesse momento, o governo tem de agir de uma maneira um pouco mais forte para tentar evitar que esse processo acabe consumindo os investimentos no setor", diz.

Atualmente, apenas 3% da produção agropecuária está coberta por seguro , segundo o pesquisador.

Para Serigati, da FGV, o ajuste também precisa envolver credores e devedores. "Os credores vão demandar algum tempinho para que eles possam ajustar novamente suas carteiras de crédito rural. Do lado dos tomadores desse crédito, eles têm de ter as contas mais bem organizadas, para conseguir sinalizar as suas reais condições de pagar", afirma.

Além disso, ele explica que algumas instituições financeiras evitam esse tipo de crédito por causa do custo para operá-lo, gerado pela taxa Selic e pela percepção de risco, principalmente diante da instabilidade climática.

Na quarta-feira (30), o Diário Oficial da União publicou a lei 15.526/2026, que funcionará como um novo marco regulatório para o seguro rural no país. Ele já atende diversos dos pedidos feitos pela Abag, como a a regulamentação do Fundo de Catástrofe, voltado para os prejuízos causados pelo clima.

Além disso, a nova lei também determina que as despesas com a subvenção ao prêmio do seguro rural tenham caráter obrigatório. Para a Confederação da Agricultura e Pecuária do Brasil (CNA), isso vai vai evitar o contingenciamento de recursos e traz uma blindagem no orçamento.

Até então, o seguro rural não era uma despesa obrigatória e era uma das primeiras áreas a sofrer cortes, explica Serigati, pesquisador da FGV.

Segundo Gilio, muitas vezes, critérios previstos nas políticas de crédito rural não são cumpridos e que até linhas financiadas pelo Plano Safra são de difícil acesso para o produtor. O pesquisador diz que o governo precisa investir no setor, por se tratar de uma atividade estratégica para a economia do país.

Para os especialistas, a dependência de fertilizantes importados é, hoje, o principal problema dentro desse tema. O Brasil importa cerca de 80% dos adubos químicos que consome, e parte relevante dos fornecedores está em países envolvidos em guerras ou em rotas afetadas por conflitos, como o Estreito de Ormuz .

O Brasil já conta com o Plano Nacional de Fertilizantes, que busca aumentar a independência do país nessa área. No entanto, seus resultados são de longo prazo. Além dos investimentos, é necessário que haja fontes de potássio, fósforo e nitrogênio disponíveis para exploração.

"A gente tem matéria-prima para alguns produtos, mas, para outros, a gente não tem. Vamos continuar dependendo de um certo volume de importação", diz Carlos Eduardo de Freitas Vian, da Escola Superior de Agricultura Luiz de Queiroz Esalq- USP .

Enquanto o plano não é concretizado, o Brasil deveria diversificar os fornecedores, para ficar menos exposto aos conflitos, afirma Serigati, da FGV. A Abag também pede para aumentar a fabricação de maquinários no Brasil. Contudo, o pesquisador afirma que o país até exporta esses itens.

Para Vian, a principal dependência está nos componentes dos maquinários, como os chips. Na avaliação dele, é inviável trazer esse tipo de fabricação para o Brasil, já que o país não teria demanda suficiente.

O documento da Abag também cita um "passivo regulatório" que atrasa a aprovação de novas tecnologias. Nesse caso, o professor da Esalq acredita que, de fato, isso acontece na aprovação de defensivos químicos, por causa da realização de testes de segurança, tanto ambientais, como para a saúde.

"Porque quando você agiliza esses processos, você pode estar deixando de visualizar alguma outra coisa. Então é um problema mesmo que, para mim, é de difícil solução", afirma.

O Brasil enfrenta um grande desafio quando se fala de infraestrutura para que em apenas um mandato presidencial consiga se resolver, afirma Serigati.

"Estamos falando de, em um prazo de quatro anos, um aumento de quase 100 milhões de toneladas, equivalente à safra da Argentina. A infraestrutura tem muita dificuldade de crescer no mesmo ritmo que a produção agropecuária", diz.

Entre os principais gargalos logísticos estão a baixa capacidade de armazenamento e as condições precárias de parte das estradas.

"É uma questão bastante grave, que eleva muito o custo e que acaba atingindo diretamente a margem do produtor agrícola e isso requer também uma ação pública", afirma Gilio.

A falta de armazenamento adequado também provoca perdas de produtos agrícolas . Um dos entraves apontados pelo pesquisador é a demora na concessão de licenças ambientais para obras.

"Porque às vezes os projetos ficam simplesmente parados, são produtos que às vezes são urgentes, já têm às vezes financiamento para fazer, já têm estudos ambientais feitos, e aí, dentro da máquina pública, essas licenças acabam ficando presas", afirma.

Outra melhoria que ele acredita que poderia ser feita é a maior integração entre os modais de transporte, como ferrovias e hidrovias, reduzindo a dependência das estradas.

Para Vian, da Esalq, a conectividade no campo também é um gargalo de infraestrutura. "Não adianta nada se você tem uma máquina conectada, se você não tem como transferir dados", afirma.

Mais de 1,3 milhão de domicílios rurais não tinham acesso à internet em 2024, o equivalente a 15% do total, segundo dados do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE).

O pesquisador do Insper pontua ainda que se trata de um problema de décadas e que levaria tempo para ser solucionado. Além disso, a iniciativa privada também precisaria investir nisso. No entanto, ele acredita que o próximo presidente poderia criar uma política de Estado voltada a garantir segurança jurídica para os investimentos.

Serigati explica que o financiamento de obras de infraestrutura é mais complexo e que o setor público não dispõe de recursos suficientes para atender toda a demanda. Por isso, a participação da iniciativa privada também seria necessária.

"E aí os instrumentos são variados: concessão, privatização ou parceria público-privada", afirma.

Comunicação e valorização da agroindústria

O agronegócio enfrenta um problema de imagem dentro do próprio Brasil e no exterior, pontua Vian. Para ele, o setor precisa realmente de um plano de comunicação que valorize seus pontos fortes, mas que também demonstre disposição para corrigir fragilidades.

Segundo o professor, o governo federal já conta com mecanismos voltados a esse objetivo, mas eles podem ser aprimorados. "Eu acho que a gente precisa preparar melhor os nossos representantes, embaixadores, para falar de uma forma institucional, mas acho que a iniciativa privada, as associações, todo mundo de alguma maneira tem o seu papel nisso", afirma.

Para Serigati, uma política pública articulada com iniciativas do setor ajudaria a posicionar o Brasil nas negociações com outros países e ampliar a abertura de mercados.

Gilio afirma que outros países têm mais sucesso que o Brasil em criar uma marca internacional dos seus produtos agrícolas. "A gente tem alguns exemplos claros, como o café colombiano", diz. "Esses produtos passam a ser desejados pela própria origem", completa.

De acordo com o pesquisador do Insper, cabe também ao setor cumprir as políticas públicas, como a de combate ao desmatamento, para colaborar com a imagem. Ele ressalta que essa não é uma ação que possa ser concluída por um único governo e que seus resultados demandam vários anos.

Inserção internacional e competitividade

O mercado internacional vive uma nova configuração, em que, além de produzir de forma competitiva, os países precisam manter um diálogo com os compradores e esse é o desafio do Brasil neste tema, afirma Serigati.

Gilio afirma que o Brasil ainda tem poucos acordos comerciais de longo prazo. Por exemplo, o país deveria ter um acordo com a China, principal cliente do setor.

"Nesse mundo de guerra comercial, em que as barreiras crescem, as tarifas crescem por um lado, as restrições sanitárias por outro. É importante o país trabalhar um pouco mais em construir pontes para que a gente consiga garantir esses mercados", diz.

Segundo ele, os acordos geram previsibilidade, o que também favorece os investimentos privados no país. O pesquisador da Insper acredita também que o Brasil deveria se antecipar mais a possíveis restrições que os países parceiros venham a criar.

Um exemplo é o caso da proibição de antimicrobianos na produção animal , criada pela União Europeia. O Brasil só reagiu após a divulgação oficial da medida, embora ela já fosse amplamente esperada.

Outra questão é que o Brasil exporta grandes volumes, mas concentra as vendas em poucos países, o que representa um risco para o mercado.

Para Serigati, o esforço de se fazer presente nas mesas de negociação internacionais cabe ao governo, o que já tem sido feito pelo Brasil ao longo dos anos, mas também da iniciativa privada, como associações.

Vian, da Esalq, concorda que essa parceria é necessária. Ele afirma que o Brasil já conta com uma legislação sanitária e ambiental sólida e precisa defender esses pontos nas negociações internacionais.

Além disso, cada setor tem de estar preparado para as regras do país que deseja atender, afirma. Isso torna mais fácil negociar os termos das comercializações por produto, por exemplo, do que em um âmbito mais amplo, diz.

articles.title: India joins US-led group on structural excess capacity
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India has joined US and a dozen other economies, including Canada, EU, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, France, Germany and UK, on structural excess
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India has joined US and a dozen other economies, including Canada, EU, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, France, Germany and UK, on structural excess capacity in five categories - autos and EVs, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors and solar panels - which are globally dominated by China.The coalition will coordinate sectoral action and comes days after a meeting of trade ministers from G20 countries with the US taking a lead on the subject during its presidency of the grouping. Separately, the US trade representative is probing several countries, including India, for structural excess capacity under Section 301. The development is also significant as it comes weeks after US President Donald Trump met his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping."We are concerned that, absent timely and effective actions, structural excess capacity and production in these sectors will cripple our domestic industries, displace local production, destroy jobs, undermine our economies, hinder efforts to develop and industrialise, and ultimately lower the standard of living for our people," a joint statement said.The countries have sought an end to the use of non-market policies and practices that distort markets and contribute to the problem. China has for long been blamed by countries across the world for offering subsidies and dumping goods. The statement also noted that countries are taking individual action and the new group will work together "in new, dedicated sectoral platforms to further examine and take effective actions that address structural excess capacity and production in key sectors of concern"."We are committed to meeting before Dec 2026, at the technical level, to develop terms of reference; share non-confidential information and data on structural excess capacity and production, its impact on these sectors, and efforts to mitigate the damage; and identify information gaps, drawing upon work of the OECD and other sources as appropriate. We commit to exploring effective and, whenever possible, complementary actions to defend our economies from the negative impact on trade and workers created by structural excess capacity and production. Working together, we aim to create the conditions necessary so that market-oriented competition in affected sectors can thrive once again," the statement said.In 2016, in Shanghai, G20 trade ministers released a statement expressing concern about excess capacity in certain industries and its negative impacts on trade and workers, and a few months later, it was also endorsed by leaders from these countries at Hangzhou.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oil prices today: Brent slips as Trump cites 'productive talks' with Iran
articles.summary: Oil prices fell on Friday as concerns over Middle East supply disruptions eased after US President Donald Trump said Washington would not attack Iran
articles.body: Oil prices fell on Friday as concerns over Middle East supply disruptions eased after US President Donald Trump said Washington would not attack Iran before next month's US elections. He also cited progress in talks aimed at ending the conflict, which has disrupted global oil markets.Brent crude futures fell 72 cents, or 0.7%, to $103.53 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures declined 52 cents, or 0.6%, to $90.97 by 7:50 am IST.Despite Friday's decline, Brent was on track for a weekly gain after settling 4% higher on Thursday amid increased attacks earlier this week on vessels carrying crude oil out of the Middle East.WTI, however, was set for a slight weekly decline despite supply disruptions caused by a hurricane approaching the US Gulf Coast.Earlier on Thursday, Trump said Washington was having “productive discussions” with Iran and that no attack was planned before the November 3 US midterm congressional elections. His remarks came after media reports suggested he was considering military action before the polls.Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran was reviewing Washington's response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.The US continues to apply economic pressure on Iran in an effort to end the conflict, which is now in its eighth month.On Thursday, Washington imposed fresh sanctions targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels allegedly involved in transporting Iranian crude oil, petroleum products and petrochemicals.Oil prices have fluctuated this week amid growing threats to shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Before the war, the strategic waterway handled shipments equivalent to about 20% of global oil and fuel supplies.Oil markets are also monitoring Hurricane Isaias in the Gulf of Mexico. The storm has forced producers to shut in about 1.3 million barrels per day, or 62.9% of current oil production in the region, as of Thursday, according to the US Marine Minerals Administration.Oil markets have remained unsettled for more than seven months since the conflict in the Middle East began. articles.title: US 10-year Treasury yield risks hitting 6% for first time since 2000, Pimco's Ivascyn tells FT
articles.summary: Oct 9 (Reuters) - The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield could rise to 6% for the first time since 2000 as high oil prices fuel inflation concerns and worri...
articles.body:
Oct 9 (Reuters) - The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield could rise to 6% for the first time since 2000 as high ‌oil prices fuel inflation concerns and worries over the country's growing ‌public debt, Dan Ivascyn, Chief Investment Officer at bond fund manager Pimco, told the ​Financial Times.

US Treasury yields are a yardstick for global borrowing costs and asset prices. The 10-year yield has risen almost 120 basis points this year and is trading slightly below the 5.34% level it hit last week, ‌its highest since 2002.

A ⁠sharp rise from the current level of 5.29% was "feasible" in the near term, Ivascyn told FT on Friday, ⁠citing factors such as hedge funds unwinding their losing bond positions.

"It is certainly possible, even from a short-term trading perspective, given that some of the ​activity we've ​seen in the last couple of ​weeks is tied to some ‌negative technicals, some stop-out activity from the platform hedge funds and other levered investors. You can certainly get there," he said.

If Treasury yields rose further, it could weigh on riskier assets such as stocks and corporate bonds, he said, adding that a move to 5.5% or higher ‌would likely lead to "some decent weakness in ​risk markets, both credit and equity".

Global bonds ​have come under heavy ​selling pressure this year as soaring energy costs fan ‌inflation and the AI boom lifts ​economic growth, leaving investors ​positioning for an era where interest rates stay higher for longer.

Bond yields, which rise when prices fall, have consequently soared globally, ​with the US 10-year ‌Treasury yield posting its biggest quarterly rise this century for ​the three months ending in September.

(Reporting by Rajveer Singh Pardesi ​in Bengaluru; Editing by Janane Venkatraman)

articles.title: From Aden to Sanaa, Yemenis struggle to deal with soaring living costs
articles.summary: As fighting intensifies, Yemenis face a deepening economic crisis, with unpaid salaries and rising prices.
articles.body:
Sanaa, Aden and Marib, Yemen – As fighting intensifies across Yemen between the government and the Houthis, millions of people are confronting another battle far from the front lines: the deteriorating living and economic conditions in the country.

With salaries for large segments of the workforce either unpaid or irregularly disbursed – and the prices of goods and services rising – Yemen’s economic struggles have been compounded by a divided banking system that has made moving money between different parts of the country increasingly complicated.

From Aden’s struggling shoppers to displaced families in Marib and unpaid public-sector workers in Sanaa, Yemenis are being forced to make difficult choices about what they can afford, and what they must go without.

In Aden, the internationally recognised Yemeni government’s interim capital in the south, the problem is not so much a shortage of goods in markets as people’s inability to afford them.

Salaries have failed to keep pace with the rising costs of food , rent, healthcare and transport , leaving workers with little money left over at the end of the month.

The consequences are evident in the smaller quantities and cheaper products that now make up shoppers’ baskets, and the decisions they are forced to make about what to cut back on.

Bushra Abdullah Abdulwarith is a government employee in Aden. She earns 78,000 Yemeni riyals ($50) a month at the black market exchange rate while typical household food costs in government-held areas run about 130,366 riyals ($83), according to estimates by the Yemen Economic Tracking Initiative. And that’s before she factors in the cost of rent, transport, healthcare and other household expenses.

The economic difficulties facing Yemenis like Bushra illustrate how more than a decade of war has devastated the economy. According to the World Bank, real GDP per capita has fallen by approximately 58 percent since 2015.

The fragmentation of Yemen’s monetary institutions between the government and the Houthis – who have operated their own institutions since seizing the capital, Sanaa, in 2014 – along with the disruption of oil exports, and declining international assistance have all contributed to the economic decline.

Bushra told Al Jazeera that rising prices have forced many households to give up almost all non-essential purchases and cut back on some expensive basics, particularly meat. Other families, she said, have resorted to buying food in smaller quantities, sometimes on credit or loans.

The impact of rising prices is reflected not only in economic figures but also in the way people shop.

Ayman al-Maqtari, who works at a shopping centre in Aden’s Mansoura district, said that his customers now rarely buy non-essential items.

When it comes to the essentials such as rice, sugar, flour, and cooking oil, he has noticed that customers size up the price of each item before putting it in their baskets. They are also buying smaller quantities, for example, opting for a 5kg (11 pound) over a 40kg (90 pound) bag of rice.

“Many people have come to live day by day, or week by week,” Ayman told Al Jazeera, adding that more families are buying on credit when they run out of money before the end of the month.

The decline in purchasing power is also affecting commercial activity.

Across several streets and shopping centres in Aden, advertisements for discounts and special offers have become increasingly visible in shop windows and on retailers’ social media pages, as businesses attempt to attract customers and boost sales.

Weak demand, retailers say, is particularly evident for items that households can put off buying, such as clothing and household goods. A growing share of family income is spent on food, rent, healthcare and transport.

The Yemeni government approved a 20 percent cost-of-living allowance in May for public-sector employees in an attempt to ease the pressure of rising prices. But the amount is calculated based on each employee’s base salary, rather than their total pay, meaning the actual increase is relatively small for many workers.

Bushra, the government employee in Aden, said the increase has done little to improve her family’s financial circumstances. She described the allowance as “a temporary painkiller that does not reflect the scale of the actual pressure on people’s living standards”.

Her experience is far from isolated. In early October, the World Food Programme said its latest monitoring in accessible government-controlled areas showed that 74 percent of households were unable to meet their basic food needs.

One of the places where the crisis is evident is Marib , a government-controlled city east of Sanaa that is home to hundreds of thousands of displaced people. The sharp increase in the population over the war years, in what was previously a provincial backwater, has led to pressure on the city’s housing, employment and public services.

Government employees in Marib see their salaries disappear within the first few days after being paid, labourers struggle to find more than a few days of work and displaced families are forced to choose between buying water and milk.

Salah al-Zuhaifi works for a government institution in Marib. He said the war has separated him from his parents, who live in Houthi-controlled territory.

Alone in Marib, al-Zuhaifi said that inflation had eroded much of his salary’s purchasing power.

“No matter how much you earn, it will not be enough to meet your needs,” he said.

Abu Mohammed Nasser al-Asbahi, another government employee, described a similar struggle.

He told Al Jazeera that he earns 400,000 riyals ($250) a month, but more than half of that goes towards his rent, leaving little for his other expenses.

“We don’t even get to the first one-third of the month before the salary is gone,” he said, explaining that his family spends the rest of the month relying on loans and credit from local shops.

The healthcare sector in Marib has also been affected by widespread household spending cuts.

Pharmacist Khaled Mohsen told Al Jazeera that the rising price of medicines has prompted many patients to decline parts of their prescribed treatment and purchase only what they consider most essential.

People with chronic illnesses, meanwhile, have increasingly begun reducing their medication doses to make their supplies last longer before having to buy more, which creates serious health risks.

Residents of Sanaa and other areas of Yemen’s populous northwest, controlled by the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – since 2014, are also facing a worsening economic and cost-of-living crisis similar to that affecting Yemenis elsewhere in the country.

Several factors are driving the crisis, particularly unpaid public-sector salaries, declining purchasing power, rising prices for goods and services, and the continuing consequences of the division of Yemen’s currency and banking systems in the early years of the war.

Many public-sector employees in Houthi-controlled areas have gone years without receiving regular salaries, with some sectors only receiving limited payments or half-salaries at irregular intervals.

Even when payments are made, they cannot cover families’ basic needs amid the rising cost of living.

Meanwhile, private-sector workers and business owners face growing pressures as a result of declining economic activity, multiple fees and levies, and a shortage of employment opportunities. The conditions have undermined incomes and job security.

The Yemeni riyal’s exchange rate in Houthi-controlled Sanaa is more stable than in areas controlled by the government. The Houthis have imposed strict monetary controls, banning the circulation of newer banknotes printed by the Yemeni government, and have also enforced a largely fixed exchange rate.

However, that does not necessarily translate into stronger purchasing power. Markets face difficulties caused by cash shortages and the division between monetary and banking systems operating in different parts of the country, including increased costs for moving funds.

That directly affects the many households relying on domestic and international remittances.

For residents in Houthi-controlled areas, the result is an economy in which the currency may be relatively stable, but livelihoods are precarious. Years of unpaid salaries and limited employment opportunities have left many families struggling to afford basic necessities, with few options beyond borrowing, cutting spending or relying on support from relatives.

articles.title: Passenger trains being run with slower freight engines as Indian Railways faces locomotives shortage; records show 80-100 cases a month causing delays of several hours
articles.summary: Indian Railways seems to be running short of locomotives to run its passenger trains, prompting the national transporter to make use of locos for freight
articles.body: Indian Railways seems to be running short of locomotives to run its passenger trains, prompting the national transporter to make use of locos for freight trains. A shortage of locomotives meant for passenger services has forced Indian Railways to deploy slower freight engines on passenger trains, resulting in delays running into several hours, according to railway records.The Railway Ministry, however, said it was accelerating efforts to expand locomotive production. It has approved 492 passenger locomotives for 2026-27 and another 187 for 2027-28, taking the total to 679 over the two financial years.“The 2026-27 programme includes 326 WAP-7 locomotives and 166 WAP-7 locos. Besides these productions in the pipeline, there is a rapid adoption of modern trainsets and improvement in utilisation of existing assets,” a senior official from the Ministry told PTI.The official added that train operations had expanded manifold over the past 12 years, and Indian Railways was making every effort to provide a safe and comfortable journey to passengers across all categories.Also Read | Delhi-Varanasi in less than 4 hours, Mumbai-Pune in 48 minutes, Chennai-Bengaluru in over 1 hour: Indian Railways bets on seven new bullet train corridors in Rs 16 lakh crore high-speed pushDelays of several hoursRailway records quoted in the PTI report contain several instances in which a lack of locomotives designed for passenger services led to trains being hauled by freight engines, which operate at lower speeds. The use of these locomotives has affected running times and caused operational delays, the records show.Officials confirmed that railway zones across the country report an average of 80 to 100 such incidents every month.One recent case involved Train No. 11044, the Ballia-Dadar Central Express, whose operations were disrupted on September 3, 2026, for 5 hours and 28 minutes because the required passenger locomotive was unavailable, according to railway records.The train was scheduled to operate with a WAP-4 passenger locomotive, capable of running at speeds exceeding 130 kmph. However, North Eastern Railway arranged a freight locomotive certified for speeds of up to 100 kmph because a suitable passenger engine was not available.“The train subsequently suffered loss on run in the Bina–Khandwa section between 13:26 hrs and 00:59 hrs. The incident resulted in a recorded detention of 328 minutes (5 hours 28 minutes),” sources told PTI.Also Read | Second Vande Bharat sleeper set to launch this month between Bengaluru and Mumbai; cutting travel time from 24 hours to under 16 hours, 30 year wait for faster connectivity between two cities to endIndian Railways’ locomotives fleetData for September 2026 show that Indian Railways has approximately 17,900 locomotives in its fleet. Of these, around 13,700 are electric engines, while roughly 4,200 run on diesel.Of the approximately 13,700 electric locomotives in Indian Railways' fleet, around 3,400 are passenger engines belonging to different variants of the broad-gauge AC electric WAP series. The remaining locomotives are from the WAG series, designed primarily for freight services and associated operational requirements.Among the 4,200 diesel locomotives, 284 are deployed for passenger services. Most of the others are used for freight transportation, shunting, departmental work and other duties.Indian Railways data show that its locomotive fleet comprised 10,456 engines in 2013-14, including 5,633 diesel and 4,823 electric locomotives. Of the electric engines, 1,371 were passenger locomotives. However, the data for that financial year do not specify the total number of diesel locomotives used for passenger services.Railway officials said the expansion of electrification from 2014 onwards gradually slowed diesel locomotive production, while manufacturing of electric engines gathered pace.Instances of freight locomotives being deployed on passenger trains have been reported across almost every railway zone in the country.On September 21, 2026, records showed that at least two passenger trains were operating with WAG-9 freight locomotives, which have a maximum running capacity of 100 kmph. The substitution was necessary because passenger locomotives capable of running at higher speeds were unavailable.In one such case, Train No. 14102, the Kanpur Central-Prayagraj Sangam InterCity Express, was assigned a WAG-9 freight locomotive with a running capacity of 100 kmph.According to sources, the train was scheduled to run with a WAP-1 passenger locomotive, which can operate at speeds of up to 130 kmph.“Due to shortage of passenger locomotives, the rail administration has to substitute it with freight engines. This led to a delay of at least 30 minutes as the train operated at 100 kmph in sections where the speed permission was 130,” a railway source said.A second incident recorded on the same day highlighted similar operational difficulties arising from the use of freight engines on passenger services.Train No. 17601, which operates between Kacheguda in Telangana and Shri Ganganagar in Rajasthan, was assigned a WAG-9 freight locomotive instead of its scheduled WAP-7 passenger engine because of a shortage. The substitution resulted in a detention and affected the train's overall punctuality.“The production of locomotives has increased manifold in the last 12 years. articles.title: If the Strait of Hormuz is open, why are gas and diesel so expensive?
articles.summary: The Strait of Hormuz is no longer paralyzed and yet fuel prices remain painfully high. It’s a vexing problem with profound financial, political and economic consequences.
articles.body: The Strait of Hormuz is no longer paralyzed and yet fuel prices remain painfully high. It’s a vexing problem with profound financial, political and economic consequences. Gasoline prices, averaging $4.36 a gallon nationally, have never been this high at this time of year, according to AAA data. Even after a series of emergency steps from US states and Europe, diesel is only about 20 cents away from the all-time high set just last month. In short, what started as an oil supply crunch caused by the Iran war has morphed into a broader energy crisis being felt by drivers, truckers and farmers around the world. Unblocking the Strait of Hormuz has been helpful, but it’s still incredibly dangerous – and thus expensive. Not only that, but Russian refineries are getting destroyed by Ukrainian drones, and Houthi attacks in the Red Sea have disrupted a vital shipping lane. “The wars have not been resolved. There is no peace. The energy system is still constricted,” said Jan Stuart, global energy strategist at Piper Sandler. ‘Insane’ cost of oil supertankers The security challenges have been underscored by the staggering cost of getting crude oil out of the Middle East. Last year, the daily cost of hiring an oil supertanker (known as a Very Large Crude Carrier, or VLCC) to sail from the Persian Gulf to China was just $65,000, according to Clarksons, a London-based research firm. By the time the Iran war was about to begin, that cost had climbed to $230,000 per day. Now? It costs $1.6 million per day to hire a VLCC for that route, according to Clarksons. “That’s insane,” said Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser at Gulf Oil. “If you own a tanker, you’re in great shape – as long as it goes unscathed by the war.” But some tankers are not emerging unscathed. Multiple commercial vessels reported getting struck by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz in recent days alone, including at least two crude oil tankers, according to the United Kingdom’s Maritime Trade Operations. Insurance, sailor costs surge But it’s not just the cost of hiring a tanker. It’s the cost of persuading sailors to go on dangerous voyages in war zones. Some shippers are offering sailors up to $25,000 per trip – an amount that could represent more than a year of wages, according to The Wall Street Journal. Insurance costs have also skyrocketed, reflecting the risk of sailing through the region with valuable cargo. Oil producers are now paying between $30 million and $40 million for a roundtrip voyage in and out of the Strait of Hormuz, the Journal reported. Real-world vs. financial price All of this – the cost to hire a tanker, exorbitant payments to sailors and surging insurance rates – is making it more expensive for consumers and businesses around the world. It used to cost just $2 per barrel to get crude out of the Persian Gulf. Now, that cost has spiraled to about $33, according to Kloza. “We’re getting a reasonable amount of crude out, but that’s misleading because the cost of that crude exiting is incredible,” he said. This helps explain the wide gap between the price of crude in financial markets and the price in the real world. Consider that the price of Dated Brent – the real-world cost of receiving immediate physical barrels of crude – is $135.74 a barrel as of Thursday, according to S&P Global Platts. That’s well above the Brent futures price of about $100 and not far from the all-time high set in April. And it’s that real-world price that trickles down to what consumers are paying at the gas station. “The United States does not live in isolation. We live with a global price because we import gasoline,” said Stuart. Refineries are getting blown up The global energy system is not experiencing a single war, but two or arguably three wars – simultaneously. On top of the US-Iran war, a conflict that has stretched for much longer than many imagined when it started, there is the battle between Yemen and Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Houthi drone and missile attacks have disrupted another vital chokepoint for global trade, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. And then there are the increasingly successful Ukrainian drone attacks destroying refineries in Russia, one of the world’s leading exporters of diesel. Facing fuel shortages at home, Russia has responded by limiting its fuel exports. China, seeking to avoid shortages of its own, has similarly restricted its exports. US refineries are the only ones left standing. But they are already producing as much gasoline, diesel and jet fuel as they can. Now, some US refineries are dialing back their production for routine maintenance that typically occurs at this time of the year. Hurricane Isaias could make matters worse if the storm knocks production offline or damages refineries along the US Gulf Coast. Buffers have vanished Energy prices would be much, much higher if not for the fact that the world had a sizable rainy day fund built up when the year started. Commercial and emergency stockpiles act as shock absorbers during crises. But now those inventories have been aggressively drawn down, leaving the world with less margin for error now. Those shrinking stockpiles have driven up the premium built into current prices. “We are running on very, very low inventories. We don’t have buffers anymore,” said Stuart. All of this explains why prices remain high and the risks are elevated – even as the flow of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz has recovered towards pre-war levels. “You have to end all three wars – or even two out of three wouldn’t be bad,” said Kloza.
